newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Nov 19.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Nov 19.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BARCLAYS IN TALKS WITH CABLE TV COMPANIES

Barclays Bank is in discussions with cable companies about plans for a new decoder box, which will unscramble digital signals. Cable companies are hoping to wrest control from BSkyB, which has a huge influence on the content and distribution of pay-television. High street banks are keen to test the demand for interactive banking, and the cable companies need to find partners who will help subsidise the cost of the decoder box.
-- MIDLAND DENIES SNUB FOR MALAYSIAN CHEQUE

Malaysian Prime Minister, Mahathir Mohamad, has accused Midland, bankers to Lotus, of trying to block the sale of 80 percent of the company to Proton, the Malaysian car manufacturer, by insisting on a cash payment, rather than a cheque, to complete the 64 million stg deal. Midland denies any snub or questioning the credit worthiness of the company and claim there has been a misunderstanding.
-- BRITISH AIRWAYS PREPARES GROUND FOR AN INCREASE IN AIR FARES

British Airways is seeking official clearance, from the Civil Aviation Authority, for further fare increases averaging two and a half percent to recover the latest rise in fuel costs following recommendations from the international air industry cartel Iata. The company has already raised fares by up to three percent on a variety of international routes. The jump in the cost of duty free aviation fuel reduced BA's interim profits by 51 million stg and the company has warned there will be further setbacks in the second half.
THE TIMES
-- STUNNING TAX HAUL IMPROVES CLARKE'S HAND

A stunning haul of tax receipts in October means that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has more room to manoeuvre in the Budget, however, the City has given a warning that tax cuts would be inappropriate when the economy is showing robust growth. Corporation tax receipts meant the Government paid back 4.39 billion stg of borrowing in October, helped by a bounce back in VAT and excise duties, which reflect healthy consumer spending. The City and Treasury believe the Government is back on track to meet its 26.9 billion stg forecast for the public sector borrowing requirement this year.
-- GEORGE DEFENDS ROLE AS WATCHDOG

Eddie George, governor of the Bank of England, Michael Foot, an executive director of the Bank, and Ian Watt, an advisor, have defended the Bank's role as a watchdog after hostile questions from members of the Commons Treasury Select Committee, which is conducting an inquiry into the collapse of Barings. Mr George described accusations of complacency as being "offensive".
-- TELEKOM DIALS INSTANT PROFIT

The flotation of Deutsche Telekom on the New York and Frankfurt stock exchanges has lead to investors in the German telephone group sharing instant paper profits of 1.4 billion stg. Some 38 million Telekom shares changed hands and German traders said the floatation had resulted in one of the busiest days in the bourse's history. Analysts predict that shares will plot an erratic course over the next few days before finding a more stable trend.
THE GUARDIAN
-- RAIL FIRM TO CUT 3,000 JOBS

Ed Burkhardt, chairman of the English, Welsh and Scottish Railway, Britain's largest privatised freight rail company, is set to cut 3,000 of its 7,000 staff over the next three years in an attempt to turn loss-making into profit. He claims the wide- ranging job cuts were necessary to make the company competitive. The cuts are not expected to meet much resistance from the unions, which have had to accept 10,000 job losses since the industry was privatised.
-- GRID UNLOCKS OLD POWER STATION

National Grid, Britain's largest electricity generator, has ordered National Power to recommission its oil-fired power station in South Wales, amid concern that supplies could be inadequate. The move comes amid a growing row over a Government- backed scheme to allow gas-fired power stations to operate using expensive back-up fuel and to pass the costs through to customers.
-- MATTEL BUYS UP TYCO'S TOYBOX

Toymaker Mattel, the American group best known for Barbie dolls, has agreed to pay 755 million dollars to buy Tyco, America's third biggest toy manufacturer who own Matchbox cars and Sesame Street characters. The deal will increase Mattel's sales to five billion dollars a year, giving it a lead over Hasbro, maker of Action Man and Monopoly. The combined group will have about 19 per cent of the US market alone and the deal could be completed next year.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- MASTERCARD BUYS STAKE IN MONDEX

The idea of a cashless society moves closer with the news that MasterCard International is set to buy a 51 per cent stake in the "electronic purse" designed by NatWest, Mondex, in a deal worth 150 million dollars. Mondex has designed the technology which will replace the magnetic strips currently used on the debit and cash cards in Britain and the rest of the world. MasterCard is now committed to using that technology in the 370 million credit and debit cards in circulation world-wide.
-- OFTEL CHIEF HINTS AT BRITISH TELECOM CONTROLS

Telecommunications regulator Don Cruickshank has given a clear signal that he will seek new controls over British Telecom's UK operations to safeguard investment and service standards for British consumers. He gave a glowing view of BT's transformation from a state-owned monopoly to a global contender capable of mounting the UK's biggest takeover. However, he is concerned that after the deal went through BT would still provide enough cash to give UK customers a fair deal.
-- THORN RESULTS PROMPT SHARES TO SLIDE BY TEN PERCENT

Shares in Thorn have fallen by ten percent in a reaction against the electrical retailer's first set of results since demerging from music publishing giant EMI. Thorn are cautious about the outlook on both sides of the Atlantic. Chief executive Mike Metcalf blamed Thorn's poor stock market performance on worries about litigation in the US and that the company would contest any damages award from lawsuits it faces in several states over its rental-purchase sales system.
